stances.claim: The sheer number of ATA petitions (27 and counting), while demonstrating the breadth of public outrage, will paradoxically delay rather than accelerate the Court's ruling because the justices must read over 2,000 pages of petitions plus thousands more of OSG comments, replies, memoranda, and forthcoming IRR challenges.

stances.claim: The Court is legally 'blind' to the number of petitioners and their political/social stature, weighing issues only on the merits -- so petitioners gain no advantage from filing separately and lose ground to the disciplined single-voice OSG.
stances.rhetorical_move: quality-over-quantity doctrinal reminder (institutional norm as procedural advice)

stances.claim: The pragmatic solution proposed by Romulo Macalintal -- consolidating all petitions into one united pleading with chosen lead counsels mirroring the OSG's single-counsel structure -- is the only realistic way to avoid a years-long delay that would let ATA's alleged perils unfold while the case sits pending.

stances.claim: Petitioners must set aside ego and media soundbites -- forgetting filing order or who raised the more cogent arguments -- to pick lead lawyers with 'tested ingenuity and experience,' because in this combat against a unified OSG, fragmented advocacy is self-defeating.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban welcomes the Supreme Court's signal that it intends to fast-track the petitions challenging the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 by setting oral argument for the third week of September 2020 at the earliest. But he warns that the sheer volume of pleadings -- 27 separate petitions averaging 75 pages each (over 2,000 pages total), the OSG's 223-page Comment for the first nine, forthcoming replies and memoranda, plus the IRR challenges still to come -- will ironically slow rather than speed the case, potentially beating the 1,000-page record set by Republic v. Sereno (May 11, 2018) and dragging the case beyond justices' retirements. To break the delay, he reproduces and endorses lawyer Romulo Macalintal's proposal that petitioners consolidate all their separate suits into one united pleading with agreed lead counsels, mirroring the OSG's single-counsel structure under Solicitor General Calida. He urges petitioners to 'set aside their ego and media soundbites,' choose counsel of 'tested ingenuity and experience,' and avoid the paradox that prolonged litigation would expose Filipinos to the very ATA perils the petitions seek to prevent.
